newsitem.title: USA: Ford agrees to $350 million Budget Rent a Car deal.
newsitem.headline: Ford agrees to $350 million Budget Rent a Car deal.

text.p: Ford Motor Co. said Tuesday it agreed to sell its interests in Budget Rent a Car Corp. to a Florida company for about $350 million.
Team Rental Group Inc., the Daytona Beach-based buyer, already owns and operates 13 Budget franchises with 155 locations. It also leases commuter vans in 22 states and sells used vehicles.

"In light of investor interest in the entire rental car industry, we concluded that it is now in the best interests of Budget and Ford if Team Rental, Budget's largest franchisee, were to acquire Budget. It's a good fit," Ford Vice Chairman Ed Hagenlocker said in a statement.
The deal, which is expected to close in March, means Ford joins other U.S. automakers in exiting the battered rental car business.
General Motors Corp. and Chrysler Corp.. in recent years have also sold off rental car operations to a new breed of investors.

"That industry has gotten a little fat. They sit with a lot of cars that go unrented. And when that happens, the bottom line is destroyed," said George Magliano, automotive consultant at WEFA Group in New York.
Lisle, Ill.-based Budget, together with its independent licensees, ranks as the world's fourth-largest rental car business, Ford said.
Ford does not own Budget outright, but controls it through a stock purchase option.
"We have the right to direct the sale of the common shares and that's what we have done," spokesman Chris Vinyard said.

A Team Rental spokesman said the company will pay $275 million in cash and issue non-voting preferred securities convertible into 4.5 million shares of Team common stock with a minimum value at closing of $75 million.
The board of Team Rental already has approved the deal, spokesman Steve Polito said.
Ford said it will continue to be a major supplier of cars and trucks to Budget's fleet. The transaction also includes a new vehicle supply arrangement between Ford and Budget.

Ford also owns Hertz Corp., the world's largest rental car agency. The automaker said this month that it was reviewing strategic options for Park Ridge, N.J.-based Hertz, which could include a partial sale.
But Hagenlocker said then it was "premature to determine whether any actions concerning Hertz will occur, or if they do, when they would occur."
Automakers began acquiring rental car companies in the mid-1980s with the idea that they could absorb unsold auto inventory into their fleets.
That strategy worked for a few years, but then backfired when sales of barely used rental vehicles began eating into new car sales.
"Automakers are now looking to exit their rental interests in a benign way," said A.G. Edwards auto industry analyst Michael Braigg in St. Louis.
Wall Street analysts said they expected Hertz to be sold, spun off or taken public by Ford.
In addition, they said, they expect Chrysler may soon sell its Dollar Rent-A-Car unit. Chrysler sold off Snappy Car Rental in 1994.
General Motors sold its stake in Avis Inc. last June after selling National Car Rental Systems in 1995.
Ford's stock gained 50 cents to $33.75 in late morning trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
